newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota suspends production as strategy backfires.
newsitem.headline: Toyota suspends production as strategy backfires.

text.p: A weekend fire at a car parts supplier forced Japanese car giant Toyota Motor Corp to suspend most of its domestic production for a full day on Tuesday.
The accident cast a spotlight on Toyota's famous "just in time" production system, which in the best of times boosts production efficiency by notches.
But analysts said its popular strategy, under which parts makers supply parts just prior to car assembly instead of keeping them in storage, backfired this time by causing a serious auto part crunch.

A fire at Toyota group company Aisin Seiki Co Ltd on Saturday halted output of brake parts supplied to Toyota, forcing it to announce the closure of all but one domestic plants for a full day on Tuesday.
Aisin, which ships about 90 percent of its products to Toyota, said it would be unable to supply some brake-related products as it had no alternative production facility.

Hideaki Aonuma, an industry analyst at Societe Generale Securities, said despite the crisis, Toyota was good at managing risks and would ask its other group companies to provide the necessary car parts.
"The remaining issue for Toyota is how to get necessary materials," he said.

Toyota, which usually produces about 14,000 cars per day at its 12 plants in Japan, closed one factory in Kyushu, southern Japan, on Monday. Its production plan after Tuesday will be decided later, a Toyota spokesman said.
The spokesman said Toyota's overseas production would not be affected by the suspension. The suspension would likely affect exports but he declined to comment on any estimate,
Toyota officials declined to estimate any likely damage from the suspension, but private analysts believe Toyota's bottom line will not suffer any major ill effects.

"The damage appears to be not as serious as we had thought," said Seiji Sugiura, a car analyst at Nomura Research Institute. "Because there was no damage to the moulds for the brake parts, it may not take much time for Aisin to resume output."
Sugiura said he had no plan to revise his own forecast for Toyota's parent current profit of 615 billion yen ($5.04 billion) in the year to March 1997.
Societe Generale's Aonuma said: "An output suspension for a few of days or even a week is unlikely to cause any decline in Toyota's earnings to below the company's forecast this financial year."
Toyota in November forecast a parent current profit of 550 billion yen ($4.50 billion) for the year to March, up from a profit of 340.73 billion yen ($2.79 billion) the previous year.
Toyota's domestic output has so far remained at or above the company's target and the weaker yen will also help support its profits by boosting export income, Aonuma said.
Last week, Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda said the current weakness of the yen would be more positive for its business than it had expected.

On the Tokyo stock market, the news of the fire spurred active profit-taking in Toyota shares on Monday, pushing down the shares by 40 yen to 3,090 yen ($25) at the close. Shares in Aisin Seiki also shed 120 yen to end at 1,650 yen ($13).
